In light of the challenges faced by conventional objective and subjective benchmarks, we propose MMBench, a systematically designed objective evaluation benchmark to robustly evaluate different abilities of large vision-language models.
Currently, MMBench contains over 3000 multiple-choice questions covering 20 different ability dimensions, such as object localization and social reasoning, for evaluating vision-language models.
Therefore, we adopt Perception and Reasoning as level-1 (L-1) abilities in our taxonomy.
and categorize them into six L-2 and twenty L-3 ability dimensions.
The data — including images, choices, and questions — are manually collected from multiple sources by a group of volunteers.
we enlist the volunteers, all of whom are undergraduate or graduate students from various disciplines, to expand the problem set.
According to the statistics, more than 80% of questions in MMBench are collected from the Internet.
If more than half of the LLMs can answer the question correctly with text-only inputs, the question will be manually verified and then removed if it is unqualified.
If all VLMs fail to answer the question correctly, we consider this question potentially problematic.
During the process, all content in questions and choices are translated to Chinese based on GPT-4, except for proper nouns, symbols, and code.
All those translations are verified by humans to ensure the validity.
In the present study, we have gathered a total of 3,217 data samples spanning across 20 distinct L-3 abilities.
with at least 125 samples for each L-3 category.
We follow the standard practice in previous works [35] to split MMBench into dev and test subsets at a ratio of 4:6.
For the test subset, only the data samples are released, while the ground truth answers remain confidential.
To obtain the test subset evaluation results, one needs to submit the predictions to MMBench evaluation server.

In the following experiments, we adopt gpt-4-0125 as the choice extractor due to its superior alignment capability.
To this end, we introduce a more robust evaluation strategy termed Circular Evaluation (or CircularEval).
A VLM is considered successful in solving a question only if it correctly predicts the answer in all circular passes.
once a VLM fails on a circular passes, there is no need to infer the remaining passes, which makes the actual cost of CircularEval less than N × under practical scenarios.
random guessing will lead to ∼25% Top-1 accuracy for 4-choice questions, potentially reducing the discernible performance differences among VLMs.
For a fair comparison, we adopt the zero-shot setting to infer MMBench questions with all VLMs, based on the same prompt.
For all VLMs, open-ended generation is adopted to obtain the prediction, and ‘gpt-4-0125’ is used as the choice extractor.
We conduct all the evaluation with VLMEvalKit [14].
